structure.title: A household waiting
structure.text: Books 1–4 follow the family awaiting Odysseus and the pressures gathering around his absence.

structure.title: Travel and return
structure.text: Books 5–12 bring Odysseus into view and let him recount his travels. Books 13–24 concentrate on returning and establishing who belongs at home.

people.name: Odysseus
people.text: An absent king skilled in persuasion.

people.name: Penelope
people.text: His wife, under pressure to remarry.

people.name: Telemachus
people.text: Their son, learning to speak with authority.

context.title: Hospitality
context.text: A stranger should receive food and shelter before being interrogated. Hosts and guests both have obligations, and their conduct reveals what kind of society this is.

context.title: After Troy
context.text: The Trojan War is over. Odysseus has not returned, and his household lacks the certainty of either a living ruler or a confirmed death.

notice.why: The speaker's purpose shapes the account.
Identity must be demonstrated as well as announced.

opening: Odysseus has survived the Trojan War, but ten years later his wife still does not know whether he is alive. Men crowd his house, eat his livestock, and compete to replace him. Their son has grown up waiting for a father he barely knows. Meanwhile, Odysseus is stranded with a goddess who wants to keep him forever. Getting home will require the cunning that helped destroy Troy; reclaiming his place there means facing people who have spent twenty years learning to live without him.
